locations.name: Adelaide
locations.depot: container depots around Outer Harbor and the Wingfield–Gillman industrial area, topped up from the eastern seaboard when a grade or a size runs short
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–6 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, for Hills blocks and for any inner-suburban lift over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Adelaide. Reactive clay, narrow inner streets and Hills access allowed for before the truck is booked.
locations.line: Adelaide sits on some of the most reactive ground in the country, and that is the one thing worth getting right here. The clay across the plains and the older inner suburbs takes up water through a wet winter and gives it back over a dry summer, and it shifts a long way doing it. A container dropped straight onto that follows it down, one corner at a time, and a racked box is a box whose doors fight you every morning. Everything else — Hills roads, Stobie poles, narrow bluestone frontages — is solvable with a phone call. The ground needs planning.
locations.uses: trade and plant storage across the Wingfield, Regency Park, Edinburgh Parks and Lonsdale industrial estates, vintage gear and barrel storage for growers through McLaren Vale, the Barossa and the Hills, packing shed overflow for the orchards at Lenswood and Forest Range and the market gardens on the Virginia sand plains, site stores on the Mount Barker, Seaford and Angle Vale estate builds, household storage while a bluestone villa at Prospect or Norwood is gutted and reroofed, and secure gear storage on the rural blocks out through Kersbrook and Williamstown
access: Adelaide splits into three delivery problems and they barely overlap. The plains — Wingfield, Gillman, Regency Park, Edinburgh, Direk, Lonsdale — are about as straightforward as anywhere in the country. Hardstand, wide entries, room to swing a rigid truck, often a forklift already on site. Gillman and parts of the Dry Creek fringe are reclaimed ground with a firm crust over something softer, which is worth flagging if you are on a newer lot down there, but otherwise those jobs get booked and done. The inner suburbs are the second problem. Norwood, Prospect, Unley, Thebarton and the streets threaded between them were set out long before anybody imagined a twelve-metre rigid. Frontages are narrow, the cottages sit hard against one boundary with a side gate barely a metre wide, cars park both kerbs, and there is a Stobie pole standing in the verge exactly where a crane truck wants to plant an outrigger. The rear laneways look like the answer and usually are not — most are one vehicle wide, have no turning space and run a line of bins down the middle. A good number of those blocks are over-fence lifts rather than tilt-tray drops, and that is far better established at the quote than at the kerb. The third is the Hills, which needs its own conversation. Underneath all of it sits the clay. From the inner east out through the northern plains the soil is strongly reactive and it does not move evenly — more at the edges of a block than the middle, more under a big gum than away from one. Sand matters too. The LeFevre Peninsula, Semaphore and the western beach suburbs are sand over a shallow water table, which carries a loaded truck poorly and lets a corner casting bed itself in within a season. Tell us the ground, the frontage and where the poles sit, and the right truck turns up first time.

sections.h: Ground that moves with the season
p: Adelaide builders classify sites for reactivity for a reason, and the same physics applies to a six-metre steel box sitting on the back lawn. Reactive clay swells as it takes up winter rain and shrinks back through a long dry summer, and the movement is not uniform. The middle of a block behaves differently to the edge. Ground near a mature eucalypt dries harder and drops further than ground ten metres away from it. Put a container straight onto soil and it will track all of that, corner by corner, and it does not come back up. The frame carries its entire load through four corner castings; the moment those four points stop sitting at the same height the box starts working against itself, the door end distorts first, and what was a good store becomes a two-person job to open.

The fix costs very little and has to happen on day one. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under each corner casting, bedded onto ground that has been cleared of topsoil, checked level along both sides and both diagonals. Keep the underside open so air moves and water gets away rather than ponding against the bottom rail. Where a block has any fall, put the door end on the high side so the doors swing with gravity instead of against it. Keep root zones in mind — siting a long-term container inside the drip line of a big gum is asking the clay to do its worst directly underneath you. Mention the soil at the quote and we will bring the timber on the truck and level it as part of the delivery.

sections.h: Up the face of the Hills
p: Anything above the freeway is a different job. The climbs to Stirling, Aldgate, Crafers, Bridgewater and out through Lobethal and Woodside are narrow, heavily cambered and lined with mature exotics and stringybark that hang low over the carriageway. Norton Summit Road, Greenhill Road and the older tracks off Gorge Road have hairpins a long rigid truck cannot straighten out, and there are stretches with a cutting on one side and very little on the other. A 20ft on a tilt-tray manages those climbs comfortably and covers most of what people up there actually need. A 40ft is a genuine question rather than a formality, and on some approaches the honest answer is two 20ft placed end to end, which usually gives more usable space anyway.

The driveways are the second half of it. Hills blocks tend to be steep, long and unsealed, often decomposed granite or rubble with a crown and table drains, and they hold up well in the dry and go slick within an hour of a front coming through. Turning space at the top has to be real, because reversing several hundred metres downhill on a one-lane drive with a drop on one side is not a plan. Fire season adds its own layer: through summer the access tracks and the cleared areas matter to you for reasons that have nothing to do with us, and a container parked across a turnaround or an escape route is worth thinking about before it lands rather than after.

sections.h: Where an Adelaide container comes from, and whether to buy it
p: Boxes destined for Adelaide addresses come out of the depots clustered around Outer Harbor and the Wingfield–Gillman industrial area. Adelaide is a smaller container market than the eastern capitals, which has one practical consequence worth knowing: the common sizes and grades are usually sitting there, and something unusual — a particular door configuration, a specific high cube, a run of matched units — may need to come across from the east before it can go on a truck to you. That is not a problem, it is a scheduling question, and it is the difference between a realistic date and an optimistic one. Ask early if the requirement is specific and we will tell you straight whether it is a this-week job or a next-week job.

On buying against hiring, the deciding factor is almost always whether the need has an end date attached. A renovation with a program, a harvest, a lease with two years left, a site store for a build — hire keeps the capital free and takes the problem of disposal off your hands. A permanent store on a yard you own, a workshop on a Hills block, a lock-up that will still be there in a decade — buy it, because a well-kept 20ft holds value and there is a real second-hand market here. Grade is the other half of the decision. Cargo-worthy units are graded wind and watertight, which is what you want for anything living outdoors with contents you would be upset to lose. The grades page sets out the differences properly; tell us what is going inside and we will point you at the right one rather than the dearest one.

faqs.q: Will a container move on Adelaide's reactive clay?
faqs.a: It will if it is placed straight onto soil. The clay across the plains and the inner suburbs swells through winter and shrinks back over summer, and it does it unevenly across a block, so a container follows the movement one corner at a time and racks out of square. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corner castings, bedded on cleared ground and levelled both ways and on both diagonals, prevent it permanently. Keep it out from under the drip line of big gums, which dry the ground hardest. Tell us the soil at the quote and we will level it on delivery.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container to Stirling, Aldgate or Lobethal?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it regularly, but the roads set the size rather than the block does. The climbs off the freeway and the older routes over Norton Summit and Gorge Road are narrow, tightly cambered and low on canopy clearance, with hairpins a long rigid cannot straighten out. A 20ft on a tilt-tray is the reliable option up top. Where the length genuinely matters, two 20ft end to end beats fighting a 40ft up the hill. Send the address, a photo from the road looking at your gate and one down the driveway, and we will give you a firm answer before anything is booked.

faqs.q: How long does delivery take in Adelaide?
faqs.a: Three to six business days is the normal window from order to on the ground for a standard unit going to an address with workable access. What stretches it is a crane booking, a grade or size that has to come across from the eastern states first, or wet weather on a Hills driveway where waiting two days beats cutting ruts through your property. If you have a fixed date — a settlement, a site start, a vintage, a removalist already booked — say so at the enquiry and the run gets built around it.

faqs.q: Can I see the container before it is delivered to my Adelaide address?
faqs.a: Our walk-in yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia in Queensland, which is not a practical trip from South Australia. So for Adelaide deliveries we do it with photographs: ask and we will send images of the actual unit on request before delivery — the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor — rather than a stock photo of something similar. If anything in those photos is not what you expected, we sort it out before a truck is booked, not after it has landed on your block.

locations.name: Canberra
locations.depot: the Sydney container depots, run down the Hume and in off the Federal Highway — the ACT has no port of its own
locations.leadTime: Usually 4–7 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for verges crowded with mature street trees
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Canberra and the ACT. Road-freighted from Sydney, with frost, condensation and wind planned for properly.
locations.line: Nothing reaches Canberra by sea. Every container in the ACT has been carted down the Hume and in off the Federal from a Sydney depot, and that road leg sets both the timing and what is genuinely available in a given week. Once it is here the city is one of the easier deliveries in the country — wide streets, deep verges, room to work a truck. The two things that catch people out are not access at all. They are the cold, which does interesting things to the inside of a sealed steel box, and the wind that comes off the Monaro.
locations.uses: tool, records and equipment storage for the trades and contractors working out of Fyshwick, Hume and Mitchell, gear stores for sporting and community clubs across Belconnen, Woden and Tuggeranong, site stores on the Molonglo Valley and Gungahlin builds at Denman Prospect, Whitlam, Taylor and Jacka, tank fittings and vineyard gear on the blocks through Murrumbateman, Hall and Sutton, hay and feed on the rural-residential country at Wamboin and Bywong, and somewhere for camping, ski and trailer gear to live once a Canberra double garage has lost that argument
access: Canberra is a planned city and it shows in the delivery. Streets are wide, corners are generous, and the verges are deep enough that a truck has somewhere to stand almost everywhere. Two things complicate that. The first is the trees. The city was planted at scale through the sixties and seventies and those plantings are now mature, so a great many residential streets sit under a continuous canopy at three to four metres with limbs reaching well over the carriageway. A tilt-tray lifting its bed needs considerably more height than a truck simply driving under them, and that catches people out on the older streets through Ainslie, Downer, Curtin, Pearce and Hughes. The second is the verge itself. Canberra nature strips are irrigated, soft in spring and sit over a lot of underground service — power, comms, stormwater pits and the irrigation lines themselves. A loaded rear axle parked on one will leave ruts at best and crack a pit at worst, and the repair lands on the property, not the driver. The newer estates in Molonglo and north Gungahlin bring the opposite pattern: narrow carriageways, cars both sides, tight culs-de-sac, and cut-and-fill blocks with thin turf over ground that has not settled. Older Woden and Weston Creek streets add shared and battleaxe driveways where the useful width is set by a neighbour's fence rather than by the road. Outside the border it changes again — Wamboin, Bywong, Sutton and the Hall district are decomposed granite driveways, long and steep in places, excellent in the dry and greasy for a day after rain. And in winter the shaded southern faces around Tuggeranong and the Molonglo hills hold black ice well past sunrise, which is why we would rather run a delivery mid-morning than first thing in July.

p: The ACT has no port and no container terminal, so every box that lands in Canberra has already done a road leg from a Sydney depot. That is not a disadvantage so much as a scheduling fact, and it explains why the honest window here is four to seven business days rather than the two or three you would hear quoted on the coast. It also means the practical selection in any given week is whatever the Sydney depots are holding plus what can be moved onto a truck heading south. If you want something specific — a matched pair, a particular door setup, a high cube rather than a standard — the earlier that is on the table the better the answer will be.

On whether to buy or hire, the road leg pushes the decision a little further toward buying than it would on the coast, simply because moving a container in and out of the Territory is a real trip in both directions. Hire still makes clear sense where the need has an end date on it: a build with a program attached, a club season, a records purge, a house being extended. Where the container becomes part of how a site works — a permanent store on a Hume or Fyshwick lot, a gear shed on a rural block at Sutton — buying usually wins. Grade is the separate question, and for anything living outdoors through a Canberra winter with contents that matter, cargo-worthy is the grade to ask for, since those units are graded wind and watertight. The grades page lays out what each one actually means.

sections.h: Frost hollows and the inside of a cold steel box
p: Canberra's winter does something to a container that a Queensland winter never will. The city sits in a series of valleys and the cold air pools in them overnight, so Tuggeranong, the Molonglo flats and the Jerrabomberra side routinely run several degrees colder than the ridges above them, with heavy frost and sub-zero mornings for weeks at a stretch. A sealed steel box in that setting cools right down overnight and then gets hit by sun on the north side by mid-morning. The air inside warms, whatever moisture is in it rises, meets a roof panel that is still cold, and condenses. People open the doors, find water on the floor and on the top of their boxes, and conclude the roof leaks. It almost never does.

The answer is airflow and what you put inside. Vents at both ends let the box breathe rather than holding a wet atmosphere all winter. Pallets under anything stored on the floor keep it out of whatever does condense. Do not load a container with damp gear, green timber, wet canvas or a lawnmower that has just come in off the grass and then shut it up for a month. Leave the doors open for an hour on a dry, still day now and then. And be a bit careful about what genuinely needs to be indoors — paper records, electronics and anything with a fabric skin do far better with a moisture absorber in there than without one. None of this is difficult, but a Canberra container that is never ventilated will teach the lesson eventually.

sections.h: The Monaro wind and which way the doors face
p: The wind here is worth taking seriously, particularly on exposed ground east and south of the city toward Bungendore, Wamboin, Royalla and the open country running down to the Monaro. It gets up quickly, it comes hard out of the north-west in spring and swings around behind a southerly change with no warning at all, and a container door is a two-metre steel sail on a hinge. A door left swung open and unlatched will get taken by a gust, and it will either bend at the hinge or shut on somebody. Every container leaves with door retainers for exactly this reason and they are worth using every single time, not just when it looks windy.

Orientation helps too. On an exposed block, facing the doors away from the prevailing north-westerly means you are not fighting the wind every time you open up, and it keeps driven rain off the seals. The same thinking applies to placement: a long side broadside to the prevailing wind on a bare paddock is a lot of surface area, and while a loaded container is not going anywhere, an empty one on a windy ridge is lighter than people assume. Set it on pads, level it properly on both diagonals, and if it is going to sit empty on open ground for months, say so at the quote and we will talk through siting it somewhere with a bit of shelter rather than on the highest point of the block.

faqs.q: Why does a container take longer to reach Canberra than the coast?
faqs.a: Because the ACT has no port and no container terminal. Everything comes off a ship in Sydney, sits in a depot there, and then does a road leg down the Hume and in off the Federal before it gets anywhere near your block. Four to seven business days is the realistic window, and a specific grade, size or door configuration can add to that if it has to be found and moved onto the right truck first. Tell us your date at the enquiry and we will tell you honestly whether it fits rather than promising a coastal timeframe we cannot hold to.

faqs.q: Will condensation be a problem in a Canberra winter?
faqs.a: It can be, and it is the most common complaint we hear from the ACT. Cold air pools in Canberra's valleys overnight, the steel drops well below the air temperature, then the morning sun warms the inside and the moisture in that air condenses on a still-cold roof. It looks exactly like a leak and almost never is one. Vents at both ends, pallets under anything sitting on the floor, nothing damp loaded in and shut up for weeks, and an hour with the doors open on a dry day now and then handles it. For records or electronics, add a moisture absorber.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a rural block at Wamboin, Bywong or Sutton?
faqs.a: Regularly. The pattern out there is consistent: long decomposed-granite driveways with a crown and table drains, a fair bit of grade, gates set at an angle to the road and turning space at the far end that needs to be genuinely truck-sized. In the dry it is a comfortable run. Within an hour of decent rain the surface greases up and a wheel that leaves the crown ends up in a drain. Send a photo from the gate looking down the drive and one of the spot itself, and tell us about any grid or culvert on the way in, and we will plan it properly rather than finding out halfway.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for a container on a block in the ACT?
faqs.a: Quite possibly, and the ACT is its own jurisdiction with its own planning rules on top of the fact that Territory land is held under lease rather than owned outright. We are not going to guess at what applies to your particular block or lease — that changes and it is yours to check before you order. The questions that usually decide it are the same ones everywhere: how long is it staying, can it be seen from the street, is it storage or is it being altered into something else, and is it a residential or a commercial site. Sorting that out first is far cheaper than shifting it later.

locations.name: Hobart
locations.depot: the Melbourne depots, shipped across Bass Strait to the north-west coast and carted down the Midland Highway
locations.leadTime: Usually 10–15 business days, and it moves with the Bass Strait sailing schedule
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where the drive allows it; crane truck for 40ft and for the steep blocks above the city
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Hobart. Honest Bass Strait lead times, steep dolerite blocks and Channel deliveries sorted before you order.
locations.line: Bass Strait is the honest answer to most questions about a Hobart delivery. Containers reach Tasmania on a sailing rather than a schedule you can lean on, then run down the Midland Highway, and that means ordering earlier than you would on the mainland. We would rather give you a real date than a hopeful one. The other half of the job is what the container lands on. Hobart is built up the flank of a dolerite mountain — the streets climb, the blocks fall away, and there is rock a spade's depth under a lot of it.
locations.uses: pen, rope and net gear for the aquaculture operators working the Channel and the Huon, cray and scallop kit at Margate, Kettering and Dover, bin and harvest storage for the cherry and apple growers through the Huon and the Coal River Valley, vineyard gear at Richmond and Cambridge, expedition and field equipment staged around Kingston and the wharves, materials and tools on the endless West Hobart and Sandy Bay renovations, firewood and forestry contractors' gear, and shack storage for places on Bruny and the east coast that sit empty half the year
access: Hobart is the steepest capital we deliver into and the older suburbs make no apology for it. West Hobart, Mount Stuart, Lenah Valley, Dynnyrne, South Hobart and the climb toward Fern Tree are narrow, pitched hard, and lined with cars parked on both kerbs because most of those houses have no off-street parking to speak of. Driveways come off the road at an angle and at a grade, and a good number of them run down to a garage under the house rather than up to a level pad. Battery Point is its own case — one-way lanes, heritage kerbs, corners a long rigid simply cannot take, and frontages measured in a few metres. Very few of those blocks are tilt-tray sites. They are crane sites, and the questions that decide them are reach, the height of the roofline in the way, whether there are service lines across the frontage and whether the street is wide enough for outriggers without shutting it. Then there is rock. Dolerite sits close to the surface across most of the western side of the city, sometimes under a few hundred millimetres of soil, sometimes as loose blocky scree on the steeper flanks. It is superb bearing ground and it is very hard to dig, which changes how a container gets levelled: you build the low side up rather than cutting the high side down, because cutting into that is a machine job and an expensive one. The eastern shore is a relief by comparison. Howrah, Bellerive, Rokeby, Lauderdale and out toward South Arm are flatter and sandier, with a few soft spots close to the water, and Brighton, Bridgewater and the northern industrial land is straightforward hardstand. Winter adds ice on the shaded southern faces and the occasional low-level snow that closes the roads to Fern Tree and up the mountain outright.

p: There is no way to make a container arrive in Hobart as fast as one arrives in a mainland capital, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. The unit is picked in a Melbourne depot, loaded for a sailing, crosses to the north-west coast and then runs down the Midland Highway to you. Every one of those legs has a schedule attached and none of them are ours to move. Ten to fifteen business days is the realistic window, and it can be shorter if the timing lines up with a sailing that is already loading and longer if it does not, or if the weather closes the Strait. What that means practically is simple: order earlier than feels necessary. If there is a fixed date on the other end — a harvest, a settlement, a build starting, a lease ending — tell us at the enquiry and we will work backwards from it rather than forwards from today.

The distance also changes the buy-or-hire calculation. Sending a hire container back across the water at the end of a job is a real movement, so short hires make less sense here than they do in Melbourne or Brisbane, while long hires and purchases both hold up well. If the container is going to be part of how a farm, a wharf-side operation or a workshop runs, buying is usually the sensible end of it. Grade is the separate call: for anything sitting outdoors in this climate with contents you need dry, cargo-worthy is what to ask for, because those units are graded wind and watertight. The grades page explains the differences properly.

The mountain and most of the ground under western Hobart is dolerite, and it turns up in three forms that matter to a delivery. Solid rock a short way down, which is superb to sit a container on and almost impossible to excavate without a machine and a budget. Loose blocky float and scree on the steeper slopes, which looks solid and rolls under load. And shallow soil over the top of either, which behaves fine until a corner casting punches through it. The consequence is that levelling here works upward, not downward. You pack and build the low side of the fall with hardwood sleepers or concrete pads until all four corners sit at the same height, rather than cutting a shelf into the high side — cutting into a slope on this ground is expensive and it creates a trench that collects water against the bottom rail for the next twenty years.

Get it right and the container carries everything through its four corner castings the way it was designed to, stays square, and keeps its doors swinging cleanly for decades. Get it wrong on a sloping Hobart block and the frame racks within a season. Put the door end on the high side of the fall. Keep the underside clear and open so air moves through rather than sitting damp against the floor bearers. And on a block with scree or loose float, spend the extra half hour finding solid bearing for each pad instead of sitting one on a rock that will roll. Tell us what the ground looks like at the quote and we will bring the packing on the truck.

sections.h: Damp, salt and a southern aspect
p: Hobart's climate is hard on steel in a quieter way than the tropics are. It is cool, it is often damp, the sun sits low for months, and a southern-facing wall or a spot under trees may not properly dry out between April and September. Add salt carried up the Derwent from Storm Bay and across the Channel, and the things that actually start corrosion are the ones that trap moisture against the metal: wet leaf litter left sitting on the roof, moss and lichen taking hold on the shaded side, long grass growing up against the bottom rail and holding it damp for months at a time. The sea air on its own does far less damage than any of those.

The maintenance list is short. Sweep the roof a couple of times a year, especially under gums and wattles. Keep the grass down around the base. Leave the underside open so air can move under the floor. Open the doors for an hour on a dry day now and then so the inside air changes over, and get vents fitted at both ends if the container is going to hold anything that minds moisture, because a sealed box in this climate will hold a damp atmosphere all winter. Where possible, site it with a bit of northern exposure rather than tucked hard against a south wall or under a permanent canopy — the difference over ten years is easy to see when you park two containers side by side.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a container to Hobart?
faqs.a: Ten to fifteen business days is the realistic window, and we would rather say that than quote a mainland timeframe we cannot meet. The unit is picked in Melbourne, loaded for a Bass Strait sailing, crosses to the north-west coast and then runs down the Midland Highway. Those schedules are not ours to move and rough weather in the Strait can add to them. Order earlier than feels necessary, and tell us any fixed date up front. Since you are buying across water, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them before delivery — corners, door end, roof and internal floor.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a steep block in West Hobart or Sandy Bay?
faqs.a: Usually, but often not with a tilt-tray. Those streets are narrow, parked out both sides and pitched hard, and plenty of the driveways drop away to a garage under the house rather than climbing to a level pad. On most of them the practical answer is a crane truck standing in the street and lifting the container over the fence or the roofline into the yard. What decides it is how far the container has to travel horizontally, what height it must clear, whether there are service lines across the frontage and whether the street will take outriggers. A photo from the middle of the road and one from the yard gets you a straight answer quickly.

faqs.q: Can you get a container to Bruny Island, the Channel or the Huon?
faqs.a: Yes to all three, and they are different jobs. The Channel and the Huon are road runs from Hobart, on roads that are narrow and winding in sections with low canopy and some tight bridge approaches, so a 20ft is a much easier proposition than a 40ft on most of them. Bruny adds a vehicle ferry from Kettering, and the operator sets the limits on vehicle length, weight and loading, so that leg gets arranged as part of your quote rather than assumed. Give us the address, the island or valley and a description of the access and we will come back with something real.

faqs.q: Will a container sweat in Hobart's climate?
faqs.a: A sealed one can, and the shaded southern side of a block is where it shows up first. Cool damp air gets shut inside, the steel drops below the dew point overnight and moisture forms on the roof and runs down. Vents at both ends make most of it go away, pallets keep stored gear off the floor, and never load damp canvas, green timber or wet gear and then close it up for a month. A moisture absorber is worth it for anything that really matters. Keep the roof clear of leaf litter and the grass down around the base and the outside looks after itself.

locations.name: Darwin
locations.depot: our own stock held at a Darwin depot, topped up off the wharf at East Arm — inspection there by arrangement
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–5 business days through the dry; rural drops stretch through the wet
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck or side loader for 40ft and for tight Palmerston frontages
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Darwin, with stock held locally. Wet season access, tropical corrosion and rural block delivery handled straight.
locations.line: Darwin runs on two calendars and a container sits in the middle of both. Through the dry everything is easy — the ground is hard, the rural tracks hold up and a truck goes where you point it. From the build-up through to April it is a different town. Black soil turns to porridge, driveways get cut, and a job that took an hour in July becomes a conversation about whether it is worth waiting a week. We hold stock at a Darwin depot rather than carting every box up the track, and that is what keeps any of this workable.
locations.uses: remote camp and mine site gear staged out of Winnellie, Berrimah and Yarrawonga, freight units heading to the Tiwi Islands, Groote Eylandt, Gove and the Roper by barge, station and community stores that have to hold a season of everything while the road is cut, packing and chemical storage for the mango and melon growers at Acacia Hills, Berry Springs and Lambells Lagoon, boat, camper and fishing gear kept out of the sun, site stores on the Palmerston estates at Zuccoli and Johnston, and dry lock-up on rural blocks where termites have already eaten one shed
access: The wet season is the first question on every Darwin delivery and it is not a formality. From November through to April the rural area behind the city — Humpty Doo, Howard Springs, Girraween, Lambells Lagoon, Acacia Hills, Berry Springs — sits on cracking black soil and heavy clay that goes from concrete-hard to bottomless within a couple of hours of a decent fall. Long unsealed driveways with a bit of grade will not hold a loaded rigid truck once that happens, low crossings go under, and a truck that gets committed to a track it cannot back out of becomes a very expensive afternoon for everybody. Laterite gravel drives hold up much better than black soil, so it genuinely helps to tell us which one you have. Through the dry, the same properties are among the easiest work we do. In town it changes shape. Winnellie, Berrimah, East Arm and the Yarrawonga industrial land are wide, hardstand, laid out for B-doubles and about as simple as it gets. The Palmerston growth suburbs — Zuccoli, Johnston, Bellamack — have the usual estate pattern of narrow carriageways, cars on both kerbs, service pits on the kerb line that will crack under a loaded rear axle, and cut-and-fill blocks with thin turf over ground that has not been through enough wet seasons to settle. The older northern suburbs have mature mango, poinciana and African mahogany hanging low over the road and short driveways with a fall at the kerb. The CBD is high-rise: loading docks, booked windows, basement height limits a truck will not meet, and building managers who need notice. And anything going to an island or a remote community adds a barge leg with its own limits on size, weight and sailing days, which we sort out as part of the quote rather than leaving with you.

p: Between November and April we plan Darwin deliveries differently, and the flexibility is built in on purpose. A rural block that took a tilt-tray straight down the driveway in August can be a no-go for three days after a decent overnight fall, and the difference between those two states is often a single storm cell that never went anywhere near the airport. We would rather ring you and move a booking than put a truck onto black soil and spend the rest of the day getting it out, because nobody comes out ahead from that — not you watching a trench get cut across your place and wondering who pays for the loader, and not us with a truck and a driver tied up.

What makes the difference is local knowledge from your end. You know whether your drive is laterite or black soil, which section holds water, whether the crossing on your road goes over and how long it takes to come back down. Tell us at the booking and we will work with it. If there is firm ground near the front — a bit of gravel hardstand, a spot by the shed that never gets soft — setting the container down there and letting you shift it in with a tractor at your own pace is frequently the cleanest answer through the wet. It is also worth knowing that we hold stock locally rather than freighting each unit up from down south, so a booking moved by a few days is a rescheduling problem, not a supply problem.

sections.h: Cyclone season, and what a container is honestly good for
p: This part gets oversold elsewhere and we will not do it. A shipping container is a strong steel box, and for keeping gear secure, dry from above and out of the weather it is very hard to beat in the Top End. It is not a cyclone shelter, it is not engineered or certified as a cyclone-rated structure, and nobody should be in one during a serious blow. It will not keep floodwater out either. A container keeps rain off from above; water that reaches the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty container is a large sealed box that will float and move if the water gets deep enough. Those are just the facts of the thing.

What that leaves is siting and sense. Put it on the highest practical part of the block rather than the flattest. Keep it clear of the overland flow path, which around Darwin does most of the damage rather than a river coming up. Do not park it directly upwind of anything you care about. Be aware that an empty container on open ground is far lighter than people assume, so if it is going to sit empty through a cyclone season, that is worth talking about at the quote — weighting it, siting it with shelter, or having it properly tied down are all worth doing and are worth doing before November rather than after a warning is issued.

sections.h: Steel, termites and a tropical climate
p: The Top End is the hardest environment in the country for a steel box, and it is the combination that does it rather than any one thing: heat, humidity nine months of the year, salt carried in off the harbour, and a wet season that keeps everything damp for months. The good news is that the things that actually start corrosion are all preventable. Wet leaf litter and mango debris sitting on the roof is the main one. Long grass and regrowth holding moisture against the bottom rail is the second. A container sitting hard on the ground with no air under it is the third. Sweep the roof, keep the grass down, set it on pads so air moves underneath and water gets away, and touch up any scratch through to bare steel before the wet rather than after it.

The other half of why containers do well here is termites. Mastotermes will go through a timber shed in the Top End faster than anywhere else in Australia, and a steel box on pads simply is not on the menu. That is a large part of why so many rural blocks out through Humpty Doo and Berry Springs end up with a container rather than a shed, along with the fact that it arrives finished and lockable on the day and does not need a slab poured and cured first. For anything living outdoors up here with contents that need to stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy — those units are graded wind and watertight. The grades page sets out what the difference is between them, and it is worth two minutes before you order.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container in Darwin before I buy it?
faqs.a: Yes. We hold our own stock at a depot in Darwin rather than freighting every unit up from down south, and inspection there is by arrangement — ring first so somebody can meet you and the unit you are interested in is accessible rather than buried behind a stack. Trading hours are Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm. If getting there does not suit, ask and we will send photos of the actual container on request before delivery: the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor.

faqs.q: Will a shipping container stand up to a cyclone in Darwin?
faqs.a: It is a strong steel box, but it is not a cyclone shelter and it is not engineered or certified as a cyclone-rated structure, so nobody should be in one during a blow. It will not hold floodwater out either — water reaching the door sill gets past the seals, and an empty container will float and move if it gets deep enough. What helps is siting it on the highest practical ground, keeping it out of the overland flow path, not putting it upwind of anything you value, and talking to us before the season if it will be sitting empty on open ground.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a rural block at Humpty Doo or Berry Springs during the wet?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it depends almost entirely on your driveway. A laterite gravel drive usually holds up. Black soil and heavy clay do not — they go from hard to bottomless within a couple of hours of a decent fall and a loaded truck committed to that track is not coming back out on its own. Tell us which one you have, whether there is a crossing on the way in and where the ground stays firm. Often the cleanest answer through the wet is setting the container down on hard ground near the front for you to shift in with a tractor when it dries out.

faqs.q: Can you supply a container to be barged to a community or an island?
faqs.a: Regularly, and it is a big part of what we do out of Darwin — units heading to the Tiwis, Groote, Gove, the Roper and stations where the road is cut for months. The barge operator sets the limits on size, weight, loading and sailing days, so that leg is arranged with them as part of the quote rather than left as your problem after you have bought a container. A 20ft is easier to move onto and around most communities than a 40ft. Tell us the destination and what is going in it and we will come back with a full answer, not just a container price.
